cues.en: So welcome to the track on NoSQL databases, although it seems like we've already had a couple of tracks on NoSQL databases. My name is Martin Fowler. Stephen Osky has hosted the track. He asked me to kick things off. Most of this track is going to be about practical experience of people making use of NoSQL databases. But this talk is the exception because this is really an introduction to what NoSQL databases are all about.
cues.zh: 欢迎来到 NoSQL 数据库专题，虽然看起来我们已经有过几个 NoSQL 数据库专题了。我叫 Martin Fowler。Stephen Osky 主持了这个专题。他让我来开场。这个专题大部分会讲人们使用 NoSQL 数据库的实践经验。但这次演讲是个例外，因为它实际上是在介绍 NoSQL 数据库到底是怎么回事。

cues.en: I'm going to do my best to cram into 50 minutes as much useful information as I can to help you give you a context for understanding a lot of what goes on in the later talks. And the first part of this is I'm going to talk a little bit about the history of NoSQL databases, because as with many things, to understand why something is the way it is, it's useful to know how on earth it got there in the first place.
cues.zh: 我会尽量在50分钟里塞进尽可能多的有用信息，帮你们建立背景，理解后面很多演讲的内容。第一部分我会稍微讲讲 NoSQL 数据库的历史，因为和很多事情一样，要理解某件事为什么是现在这样，知道它到底怎么走到这一步是很有用的。

cues.en: Now, when I started in the computer industry in the mid-80s, it was just at the point that rich relational databases were really coming in and beginning their rise. It's kind of hard to imagine that there was a time without relational databases, but I remember when they were the new hot things that people were arguing about whether there would be any good or not. And they've brought us many benefits. Obviously, they look at the persistence of our data.
cues.zh: 我上世纪80年代中期进入计算机行业时，正赶上功能丰富的关系型数据库真正开始兴起。很难想象还有没有关系型数据库的时代，但我记得当它们还是新热点时，人们在争论它们到底有没有用。它们给我们带来了很多好处。显然，它们负责我们数据的持久化。

cues.en: They're also very important in the fact that they manage concurrency through transactions. SQL has become a de facto standard language to talking to these databases. It's not entirely standard, but it's standard enough that once you know SQL, you can talk to these different tools. They've also become very important for many organisations for integration and reporting, which, as we'll see, has both its ups and downsides. So SQL databases are a really good thing.
cues.zh: 它们还非常重要，因为它们通过事务管理并发。SQL 已经成为与这些数据库交互的事实标准语言。它并不完全标准，但足够标准：一旦你会 SQL，就能和这些不同工具打交道。对许多组织来说，它们对集成和报表也变得非常重要，而正如我们将看到的，这既有好处也有坏处。所以 SQL 数据库确实是个好东西。

cues.en: But they also have some problems. And the most obvious problem is one that most application developers run into as they're working with them, which is that we assemble structures of objects in memory, often in terms of a cohesive whole of things, and then in order to save it off to the database, we have to strip out it into bits so that it goes into those individual rows and individual tables. A single logical structure
cues.zh: 但它们也有一些问题。最明显的问题是大多数应用开发人员在使用它们时都会遇到的：我们在内存中组装对象结构，往往是一个内聚的整体，然后为了把它保存到数据库，我们必须把它拆成碎片，放进一个个单独的行和单独的表中。而一个逻辑结构

cues.en: for our user interface and for our processing in memory ends up being splattered across lots and lots of tables. This is referred to as the impedance mismatch problem. The fact that we have these very two different models of how to look at things and the fact that we have to match them causes difficulties. This is what leads to object relational mapping frameworks and all that kind of stuff.
cues.zh: 用于用户界面、用于内存处理，最终却被分散到许许多多张表里。这被称为阻抗不匹配问题。我们看待事物的模型如此不同，而且又必须把它们匹配起来，这就造成了困难。正是这一点催生了对象关系映射框架以及诸如此类的东西。

cues.en: Now, the impedance mismatch problem is sufficiently of an awkward problem that in the mid-90s, people said, well, we think relational databases are going to go away. Object databases are going to come in. That way, we can take our in-memory structures and save them directly to disk without any of this mapping between the two. But we know what happened there. We didn't see the object databases, people like me who thought that they were going to be a dominant thing in the future.
cues.zh: 现在，阻抗失配问题是个相当棘手的问题，所以在90年代中期，人们说，嗯，我们认为关系型数据库会消失。对象数据库会兴起。这样我们就能把内存结构直接保存到磁盘，不用在两者之间做映射。但我们知道结果如何。我们并没有看到对象数据库成为现实，像我这样曾以为它们会成为未来主流的人。

cues.en: We were wrong. And you still listen to me. But oh well. I guess you are easily taken. But we argue endlessly about why these object databases didn't actually fulfill that potential. And I think at the heart of it is the fact that SQL databases had become an integration mechanism. That many people integrated different applications through SQL databases.
cues.zh: 我们错了。而你们还在听我讲。不过算了，我猜你们很容易被说服。但我们没完没了地争论，为什么这些对象数据库没有真正实现那个潜力。我认为核心在于，SQL 数据库已经成为一种集成机制。很多人通过 SQL 数据库集成不同的应用。

cues.en: And as a result, that really made it very hard for any other kind of technology to come in. And that led to relational continuing to be dominant right through into the 2000s. So relational had 20 years of complete dominance of certainly the enterprise data space and plenty of other ones as well. I mean, we saw the science work at the Large Hadron Collider. They didn't really want to use relational databases, but they had to, to some degree at least.
cues.zh: 结果就是，这真的让任何其他技术都很难进来。这也让关系型数据库一直占据主导地位，直到2000年代。所以关系型数据库有20年完全主导了企业数据领域，当然也主导了很多其他领域。我是说，我们看到了大型强子对撞机的科学工作。他们其实不太想用关系型数据库，但至少在一定程度上不得不用。

cues.en: What changed really was the rise of the internet and particularly sites that have lots and lots of traffic, the big internet sites such as an Amazon or a Google or a Betfair or something of that kind. As you get large amounts of traffic coming into your data, what do you do? Well, you need to scale things. And one obvious route is to scale things up, buy bigger boxes. But that approach has problems. It costs a lot.
cues.zh: 真正改变的是互联网的兴起，尤其是那些流量巨大的网站，比如 Amazon、Google、Betfair 之类的大型互联网站点。当大量流量涌入你的数据时，你怎么办？你需要扩展。一个明显的路线是纵向扩展，买更大的机器。但这种方法有问题。成本很高。

cues.en: And there are real limits as to how far you can go. So as I hope you all know, a lot of organizations, most famously Google, use a completely different approach. Lots and lots of little boxes. Just basically CPU motherboards, disks, commodity hardware, all thrown into these massive grids. But here there's an issue for the data storage. SQL was designed to run on those big boxes, designed to run as a single node system.
cues.zh: 而且你能扩展到什么程度是有实际限制的。所以，我希望你们都知道，很多组织，最著名的是 Google，用了完全不同的方法。大量小机器。基本上就是 CPU 主板、磁盘、商用硬件，全都塞进这些大规模网格里。但数据存储这里有个问题。SQL 是为那些大机器设计的，是为作为单节点系统运行而设计的。

cues.en: It does not work very well with large clusters of little boxes. And several of the big data players understood this. They tried. They attempted. I've talked to several people who have attempted to spread relational databases and run them across clusters. The usual term that comes up in conversation when they describe how they tried to do this was unnatural acts. It's very hard to do.
cues.zh: 它在大规模的小机器集群上运行得并不好。好几个大数据玩家明白这一点。他们试过。他们尝试过。我和好几个人聊过，他们尝试把关系型数据库铺开并跨集群运行。他们描述自己如何尝试时，对话中常出现的说法是“不自然的操作”。这非常难做到。

cues.en: A couple of organizations said, we've had enough of this. We need to do something different. And they developed their own data storage systems that were really quite different from relational databases. And they started talking a little bit about them, published papers that talked about what they were up to. And it is this that really inspired a whole new movement of databases, which is the NoSQL movement.
cues.zh: 有几家机构说，我们受够了。我们得做点不一样的东西。他们开发了自己的数据存储系统，和关系型数据库差别很大。他们开始稍微谈论这些系统，发表论文讲自己在做什么。正是这一点真正启发了数据库领域一场全新的运动，也就是 NoSQL 运动。

cues.en: Now, it's important at this point to talk a little bit about where this term NoSQL comes from. A lot of people complain about it, quite reasonably, because they say, well, it's a really odd term, trying to define a movement by something it's not. And the origin is really very simple. There was this guy in London, Johann Oskarsson. He'd done a lot of work with Hadoop and things like that. He wanted to have a look. He had to go to a conference in California.
cues.zh: 现在，有必要稍微讲讲 NoSQL 这个词从哪来。很多人抱怨它，而且挺有道理，因为他们说，这词很怪，想用某个东西不是什么来定义一个运动。它的起源其实很简单。伦敦有个叫 Johann Oskarsson 的人。他在 Hadoop 之类的东西上做过很多工作。他想去看看。他得去加州参加一个会议。

cues.en: He wanted to take a look at all of these various interesting databases that were poking around at the time. And he said, proposed a meetup, a little meeting where people could discuss ideas. And of course, if you're going to do that in the late 2000s, you absolutely need something that's really, really important. You need a Twitter hashtag. So he asked around, well, what would be a good hashtag? It's got to be short, it's got to be unique, so we can easily sort on it. And a guy came up with...
cues.zh: 他想看看当时冒出来的各种有意思的数据库。于是他提议办个聚会，一个小会，让大家讨论想法。当然，在 2000 年代末要做这事，你绝对需要一个非常非常重要的东西。你需要一个 Twitter 话题标签。他就到处问，什么标签比较好？要短，要独特，这样容易筛选。然后有个人想出了……

cues.en: the hashtag NoSQL. That's all NoSQL was ever meant to be. A Twitter hashtag to advertise a single meeting one point in time. The fact that it has now become the name of the whole movement was completely accidental. Nobody thought that was going to be the case. So, you know, this is the way language often goes. It's very unpredictable fits and starts.
cues.zh: 就是 #NoSQL 这个标签。NoSQL 最初就只是这个意思。一个用来宣传某一次会议的 Twitter 标签。它现在成了整个运动的名字，完全是偶然。没人想到会这样。所以，你知道，语言经常就是这样。它非常不可预测，断断续续地演变。

cues.en: So there was a whole bunch of people who turned up to that meeting, by the way. This is the list of people there. That's not what we call the whole set of NoSQL databases since. A lot of databases who weren't at that meeting are now considered part of that NoSQL umbrella. So this inevitably leads you to the question of, well, what is the definition of NoSQL? And this is something I had to kind of think about writing the book about the subject.
cues.zh: 顺便说一句，那次会议来了一大堆人。这是当时参会者的名单。这并不是我们后来称为 NoSQL 数据库的完整集合。很多没参加那次会议的数据库，现在也被归入 NoSQL 这个大类。于是这就不可避免地引出一个问题：NoSQL 的定义到底是什么？这也是我在写这个主题的书时必须思考的问题。

cues.en: It's important if you're going to write a book about something to define what it is you're writing about. My conclusion is we cannot define NoSQL databases because of this very odd history. What we can do is we can identify some common characteristics of NoSQL databases. And there's a whole bunch of ease. Obviously, NoSQL databases are not relational. It's actually more about non-relational than it is about NoSQL. Obviously,
cues.zh: 写一本关于某个主题的书，定义清楚你写的是什么很重要。我的结论是，由于这段非常古怪的历史，我们没法定义 NoSQL 数据库。我们能做的是找出 NoSQL 数据库的一些共同特征。这样的特征有一大堆。显然，NoSQL 数据库不是关系型的。它其实更强调非关系型，而不是 NoSQL 这个名字。显然，

cues.en: as a strong leading towards cluster friendliness, the ability to run on large clusters, because that's what the original Spark through Google and Amazon came from. But that's not an absolute characteristic. There are some NoSQL databases that aren't really focused around running on clusters. Most of these databases, rather interestingly, are open source. So most of the things we generally call NoSQL databases
cues.zh: 都很强调集群友好性，也就是能在大规模集群上运行，因为 Google 和 Amazon 最初带来的那波火花就源于此。但这不是绝对特征。有些 NoSQL 数据库并不真正以集群运行为核心。挺有意思的是，这些数据库大多数都是开源的。所以我们通常称为 NoSQL 数据库的大多数东西

cues.en: or open source. There are commercial tools that like to call themselves no SQL databases, and maybe over time that will become part of the, that would no longer be a common characteristic, but it is still a common characteristic at the moment. Perhaps most importantly is they're all things that have come out of the 21st century website culture. There are plenty of databases out there going back long before relational databases that do not use SQL or the relational model, but we don't
cues.zh: 都是开源的。有些商业工具喜欢自称 NoSQL 数据库，也许随着时间推移，这会不再是一个共同特征，但目前它仍然是共同特征。也许最重要的是，它们都出自 21 世纪的网站文化。有很多数据库早于关系型数据库很久就存在，也不使用 SQL 或关系模型，但我们不会

cues.en: call such things as IMS or Mumps, for those who've heard of either of those things, NoSQL databases. So that's what I see as the common characteristics. I'll mention the last one in a moment. So one of the things that's interesting about NoSQL databases is they use different data models to the relational model, obviously, since the name says that. And if we kind of plot a picture of the most
cues.zh: 把 IMS 或 Mumps 这种东西——听过这两个的人知道——叫作 NoSQL 数据库。所以这就是我认为的共同特征。最后一个我稍后再说。NoSQL 数据库有意思的一点是，它们使用不同于关系模型的数据模型，显然，名字就说明了这一点。如果我们大致描绘一下最

cues.en: commonly referred to NoSQL databases, typically what we see is that they get divided into four broad chunks based on their data model. And let's dig into these data models a little bit more. So the most simple data model to talk about is that of the key value store. The basic idea is you have a key, you go to the database, tell me, grab me the value of this key. The database knows absolutely nothing about what's in that value. It could be a single number, it could be some complex.
cues.zh: 常被提到的 NoSQL 数据库，通常我们会看到，它们按数据模型被分成四大类。我们来稍微深入看看这些数据模型。最简单的数据模型是键值存储。基本想法是你有一个键，去数据库说，告诉我，把这个键的值拿给我。数据库完全不知道那个值里是什么。它可能是一个数字，也可能是某种复杂的东西。

cues.en: document, it could be an image, the database doesn't know, doesn't care. Now you can think of this basically as just a hash map, but persistent in the disk. Simple as that. Another data model that's very common is the document data model. Now the document data model thinks of the database as this storage of a whole mass of different documents where each document is some complex data structure. Usually,
cues.zh: 文档，可能是图像，数据库不知道，也不关心。现在你可以基本把它想成一个哈希表，但持久化在磁盘上。就这么简单。另一种很常见的数据模型是文档数据模型。文档数据模型把数据库看作大量不同文档的存储，其中每个文档都是某种复杂数据结构。通常，

cues.en: That data structure is represented in forms of JSON, because JSON is what's fashionable these days. I mean, you could do it in XML, but who wants to be seen wearing XML in public? No one. So we have these different documents that all flash around. And the usual document databases will allow you to say, give me a document that has these fields with these values. You can query into the document structure.
cues.zh: 这种数据结构用 JSON 表示，因为 JSON 现在很流行。我是说，你也可以用 XML，但谁想在公开场合穿 XML 呢？没人想。所以我们有这些不同的文档四处闪现。通常文档数据库允许你说，给我一个包含这些字段和这些值的文档。你可以查询文档结构内部。

cues.en: And you can usually retrieve portions of a document or update portions of a document. So there's a big difference there to the key value store, where it's a very opaque structure, and the document is much more transparent. One thing to notice right away about these databases, about document databases, and indeed all NoSQL databases, is that they don't tend to have a set schema.
cues.zh: 而且你通常可以检索文档的一部分，或更新文档的一部分。所以它和键值存储有很大区别：键值存储是非常不透明的结构，而文档要透明得多。这些数据库——文档数据库，实际上所有 NoSQL 数据库——有一个马上就能注意到的特点：它们往往没有固定模式。

cues.en: With a relational database, you can only put the data into the database as long as it fits in the schema that you've defined for that database. With almost all NoSQL databases, basically you can shove anything in you like. Any stuff you like, just go in there. And the NoSQL people will talk endlessly about how this increases your flexibility, it makes it easier for the migrate data over time, it's all absolutely wonderful. And as usual, that's not really the entire truth.
cues.zh: 对于关系型数据库，只有当数据符合你为该数据库定义的模式时，你才能把数据放进去。对于几乎所有 NoSQL 数据库，基本上你想塞什么就塞什么。任何你喜欢的东西，直接放进去。NoSQL 的人会没完没了地讲这如何提高灵活性，如何让随时间迁移数据更容易，一切都美妙极了。和往常一样，这并不完全是事实。

cues.en: I mean, usually, when you're talking to a database, you want to get some specific pieces of data out of it. You're going to say, I would like the price, I would like the quantity, I would like the customer. As soon as you're doing that, what you're doing is you're setting up a implicit schema. You are assuming that an order has a price field. You are assuming that the order has a quantity field. You're assuming that it is called price and not cost or...
cues.zh: 我是说，通常你和数据库打交道时，是想从中取出一些特定的数据。你会说，我要 price，我要 quantity，我要 customer。你一旦这么做，就是在建立一个隐式模式。你在假设订单有一个 price 字段。你在假设订单有一个 quantity 字段。你在假设它叫 price 而不是 cost，或者……

cues.en: price to customer or whatever other thing you could think of what it would be. That implicit schema is still in place. And you've got to manage that implicit schema in many ways in a similar approach to the way that you manage the relational, more strict schema. So schema-less is really a bit of a wussy term here. Now, by having the no-fix storage schema,
cues.zh: price 还是 customer，或者你能想到的任何其他叫法。那个隐式模式仍然存在。而且你必须在很多方面管理这个隐式模式，方式类似于管理关系型那种更严格的模式。所以 schema-less 在这里其实是个有点软弱的说法。现在，通过拥有这种不固定的存储模式，

cues.en: does give you some options that you don't get with relational databases. And there is a difference. And there are advantages in terms of flexibilities as well. But you can't ignore the fact that you were always dealing with an implicit schema. The only time you don't have to worry about an implicit schema is if you do something like, give me all the fields in this record and throw them up on the screen, field name value. And occasionally you want to do that, but most of the time you actually want to do something more interesting.
cues.zh: 确实给了你一些关系型数据库没有的选项。而且是有区别的。在灵活性方面也有优势。但你不能忽视一个事实：你一直在和隐式模式打交道。唯一不用操心隐式模式的时候，是你做类似这样的事：把这个记录里的所有字段给我，然后扔到屏幕上，字段名和值。偶尔你会想这么做，但大多数时候，你其实想做更有意思的事。

cues.en: So I've talked about two data models, key value and document data models. And I've presented them as two quite different things. But actually, the line between these two is a hell of a lot more fuzzy than that. Many key value data stores allow you to store metadata about the value. This allows, of course, you to have built more complicated indexes.
cues.zh: 我刚才讲了两种数据模型：键值模型和文档数据模型。我之前把它们讲得截然不同，但实际上，这两者之间的界限要模糊得多。很多键值存储允许你存储关于值的元数据。当然，这能让你建立更复杂的索引。

cues.en: I mean, if you want to get all the orders for a particular customer, you don't want to search every order in the database to find the moral equivalent of a table scan. You want to index that. So key value databases allow you to store various metadata things, typically, which kind of makes them feel a bit like document databases, right? And then on a document database, yeah, you can do all sorts of queries against a thing, but often there's an ID.
cues.zh: 比如你想获取某个客户的所有订单，你肯定不想搜遍数据库里的每个订单，搞成类似全表扫描的操作。你想要建索引。所以键值数据库通常允许你存储各种元数据，这让它们感觉有点像文档数据库了，对吧？而在文档数据库里，虽然你能执行各种查询，但通常也有个 ID。

cues.en: And often, when you actually look that up, you actually do it by saying, give me the thing with that particular ID. And that ID is effectively the same as the key in a key value store. So the boundary between a key value and a document database, as I said, is somewhat blurry. And I've often heard a particular database sometimes described as key value and sometimes described as document. In reality, I wouldn't worry too much about the difference between them. Think of it as a kind of a first approximation.
cues.zh: 而且通常你实际查询时，也就是让它“把特定 ID 的那条记录给我”。这个 ID 实际上就等同于键值存储里的 key。所以正如我所说，键值数据库和文档数据库的界限有些模糊。我经常听到某款数据库有时被称为键值型，有时又被称为文档型。实际上，我不会太纠结它们之间的区别。可以先把它当作一种粗略的初步划分。

cues.en: to work with, but it's not actually that important as it goes on. What is important, though, is that both key value and document databases have this common notion of you're taking some complex structure that you can save as a single unit into the database. Whether it be a relatively transparent document or a completely opaque value, that notion still exists.
cues.zh: 拿来用用还行，但往后看其实没那么重要。真正重要的是，键值数据库和文档数据库都有一个共同概念：把某种复杂结构作为一个单一单元存入数据库。无论它是相对透明的文档，还是完全不透明的值，这个概念都成立。

cues.en: And that commonality made me think, well, we really need some term to describe databases that work kind of like that. And so for the book, I came up with a term, an aggregate-oriented database that allows you to store these big, complex structures. And where did the term aggregate come from? It comes from this book here, written by Eric Evans, domain-driven design. How many people have read domain-driven design? Hopefully a good few of you. Excellent book.
cues.zh: 这种共通性让我觉得，我们确实需要一个术语来描述这类数据库。所以在写书时，我提出了一个术语——“面向聚合的数据库”，它允许你存储这些庞大而复杂的结构。那“聚合”这个词是从哪儿来的呢？它出自 Eric Evans 写的这本书——《领域驱动设计》。在座有多少人读过《领域驱动设计》？希望能有不少人，那真是一本好书。

cues.en: It really talks about how to think about modeling domains. And one of the key concepts in the early part of domain-driven design is that often when we want to model things, we have to group things together into natural aggregates. Because when we're talking to a database, even a relational database, it makes sense to think of those aggregates when we're storing and retrieving data. If we're modeling orders, for instance,
cues.zh: 它深入探讨了如何思考领域建模。而在《领域驱动设计》的前半部分，核心概念之一就是：我们在建模时，往往需要把事物归类组合成自然的聚合。因为在与数据库交互时，哪怕是关系型数据库，在存取数据时考虑这些聚合也是很有意义的。比如在对订单建模时，

cues.en: Usually we'll have separate classes for the orders and the line items. That's pretty kind of a standard object 101 model. But we think of the order as a whole thing, a single unit. So an aggregate may be many objects in many classes. It may be quite a complex structure. But when we're talking about persisting it or retrieving it from memory, we think of it as one thing to cross back and forth. Now in a relational database,
cues.zh: 通常订单和订单项会有各自独立的类。这是相当标准的面向对象入门模型。但我们把订单视为一个整体，一个单一单元。所以一个聚合可能涉及很多类的许多对象，结构可能相当复杂。但当我们谈到持久化或从内存中读取它时，是把它当作一个整体来回传递的。而在关系型数据库中，

cues.en: we have to splatter that aggregate across a whole bunch of tables. But the nice thing about an aggregate-oriented database is we can save that aggregate as its single unit in the terms of the database itself. So for a key-value database, the aggregate is the value. In a document database, the aggregate is the document. And that becomes the single unit that we move back and forth.
cues.zh: 我们不得不把这个聚合打散分布到一大堆表里。但面向聚合数据库的好处在于，我们可以直接以数据库自身的存储单元，把该聚合作为一个独立单元保存下来。对于键值数据库，聚合就是那个“值”。在文档数据库中，聚合就是那个“文档”。它也就成了我们来回传递的单一单元。

cues.en: And I certainly find this is a much easier way to think about the commonality of these classes of databases. Now, the third data model I'm going to briefly describe is that of column family databases. Now, this is the more complicated data model of these. It is another aggregate-oriented database, however. The column family database basically says we have some, think of it single key, they call it a row key.
cues.zh: 我确实觉得，用这种方式去思考这类数据库的共性会容易得多。接下来，我要简要介绍的第三种数据模型是列族数据库。在这些模型中，这属于相对复杂的一种。不过，它同样是一种面向聚合的数据库。列族数据库的核心思想是，想象我们有一个单一的键，通常称为行键。

cues.en: And then within that, we can store multiple column and families, where each column family is a combination of columns that kind of fit together. The column family here is effectively your aggregate. And you address it by a combination of the row key and the column family name. Now column families can also be kind of different. Look at the lower one here. It is effectively a list of items, the various orders for a customer.
cues.zh: 然后在它之下，我们可以存储多个列族，每个列族都是一组相关列的组合。这里的列族实际上就是你的聚合。你可以通过行键和列族名的组合来定位它。列族的形式也可以有所不同。看看下面这一个。它实际上是一个条目列表，记录了某个客户的多笔订单。

cues.en: So that doesn't kind of feel so much like the typical record structure that you might know about, but it is, of course, the same as storing an array in a document and something of that kind. So again, you get something of that kind of rich structure that you can build in here. Column family databases give you a slightly more complex data model to work with, but the benefit you get is, again, in terms of the retrieval. You can more easily pull individual columns and things of that out of the case.
cues.zh: 这感觉不太像大家熟知的典型记录结构，但它当然就类似于在文档中存储数组这种形式。所以，你同样可以在这里构建出这种丰富的结构。列族数据库提供的数据模型虽然稍显复杂，但带来的好处依然体现在数据检索上。你可以更轻松地从里面单独取出特定的列等数据。

cues.en: But again, the broad data model is that of an aggregate-oriented picture. So the great thing about this is that now when you're taking your aggregate in memory, instead of spreading it across lots of individual records, you get to store the whole thing in the database in one go. And the database knows what your aggregate boundaries are. Now, this is interesting. Where it becomes really useful,
cues.zh: 但总的来说，它的宏观数据模型依然是面向聚合的。这样做的一大好处在于，当你在内存中持有聚合时，不用再把它拆散分散到多条独立记录中，而是可以一次性把整个聚合存进数据库。而且数据库也清楚你的聚合边界在哪里。这非常有意思。而它真正发挥威力的场景，

cues.en: is when we talk about running the system across clusters. Because if you're going to distribute data, what you want to do is you want to distribute the data that tends to be accessed together. And so the aggregate tells you what data is going to be accessed together. So by placing different aggregates on different nodes across your cluster, you know that when somebody says, oh, give me the details about this particular order, you're only going to go to one node on the cluster instead of shooting around goodness knows how many to pick up different rows from different tables.
cues.zh: 是我们谈到跨集群运行系统的时候。因为如果要进行数据分布式存储，你真正希望的是把倾向于一同访问的数据分布在一起。而聚合正好指明了哪些数据会被一同访问。因此，通过将不同的聚合分散在集群的不同节点上，当有人请求“帮我查下这笔特定订单的详情”时，你只需访问集群中的一个节点，而不用满集群乱转、去不知道多少个节点上拼凑来自不同表的数据行。

cues.en: So aggregate orientation naturally fits in very nicely with storing data on large clusters. And that's, of course, part of the whole thing with Bigtable and Dynamo. They both effectively went for cluster-oriented approach. Bigtable very much a column family style approach. Dynamo much more a key value store. But it makes running on clusters efficiently way more straightforward. And that's really been, as I said, the driving factor here.
cues.zh: 所以，面向聚合天然就非常契合在大型集群上存储数据。这当然也是 Bigtable 和 Dynamo 核心设计思想的一部分。它们实际上都采用了面向集群的设计方案。Bigtable 极具列族风格。Dynamo 则更偏向键值存储。但这让系统在集群上的高效运行变得直截了当得多。正如我所说，这确实是背后的核心驱动因素。

cues.en: But however, nothing is perfect. And aggregate orientation isn't always a good thing. Let's imagine we've got our order system, and we want to look at the data like this. We want to say, given a particular product, tell me the revenue, tell me a past revenue. We now not care about orders at all. We only care about what's going on with individual line items of many orders grouping them together by product. Effectively, what we're doing is we're saying we want to change
cues.zh: 但是，凡事没有完美的，面向聚合也不见得总是好事。假设我们有一个订单系统，想这样来查看数据：针对某款具体商品，看它的收入，也就是过去的收入。这时我们完全不关心订单了，只关心众多订单中的具体明细项，并按商品对它们进行分组。实际上，我们要做的是改变

cues.en: the aggregation structure from one where orders aggregate line items to ones where products aggregate line items. The product now becomes the root of the aggregate. Now, in a relational database, this is straightforward. We just query the data differently. It's very straightforward to rearrange the data into the structures we might want in different cases. With an aggregate-oriented database, it's a pain in the neck. You can do it.
cues.zh: 聚合结构，从“订单聚合明细项”变成“商品聚合明细项”。商品现在成了聚合根。在关系型数据库中，这很简单，换种查询方式就行。在不同场景下把数据重组为我们想要的结构，非常直接。但在面向聚合的数据库里，这就极其头疼了。虽然也能做到，

cues.en: And what they'll typically do is they will run MapReduce jobs to rearrange all your data into different aggregate forms and probably keep those persistent, or maybe even do incremental updates. But it's always going to be more complicated. So being aggregate-oriented is an advantage if most of the time you're using the same aggregate to push data back and forth into persistence. It is a disadvantage if you want to slice and dice your data in different ways.
cues.zh: 但通常的做法是运行 MapReduce 任务，把所有数据重构成不同的聚合形式，并持久化保存，甚至还要做增量更新。但这无论如何都会变得更复杂。所以，如果你大多数时候都是用同一种聚合结构在持久层来回读写数据，面向聚合就是优势；但如果你想从不同维度去切分和多角度分析数据，它就是劣势。

cues.en: So, what I've done so far is I've managed to cover some of these models. I've basically taken the document, column family, and key value and lumped them together under this aggregate-oriented category. And I think that's a useful abstraction, at least at the level of what I can say in 50 minutes. There's one very noticeable outlier that you see, though, and that is graph databases. Graph databases are not aggregate-oriented at all. They use a completely different data model.
cues.zh: 到目前为止，我已经介绍了一部分模型。我基本上把文档、列族和键值数据库都归到了“面向聚合”这一类。我觉得这是一种很有用的抽象，至少在 50 分钟的分享里很实用。不过，大家会看到一个非常明显的特例，那就是图数据库。图数据库完全不是面向聚合的，它们采用了一种截然不同的数据模型。

cues.en: A graph database is data model is basically that of a node and arc graph structure. Not a bar chart or anything like that, but just nodes and arcs. Something that hopefully would be familiar at least from a few boring computer science classes. The nice thing about storing a graph database is that it's very good at handling moving across relationships between things.
cues.zh: 图数据库的数据模型本质上就是由节点和边构成的图结构。不是柱状图那种图表，而是纯粹的节点和边。希望大家至少在那些枯燥的计算机课上对它有所了解。使用图数据库的好处在于，它非常擅长处理事物之间跨越关系的操作。

cues.en: Relational databases, you might think with the word relation in there that they're good at handling relationships. But of course, relation doesn't mean relationship. It means something in set theory. And actually, relational databases are not terribly good at jumping across relationships. You have to set up foreign keys. You have to do joins. If you do too many joins, you can get in a mess.
cues.zh: 至于关系型数据库，你可能会望文生义，以为带有“关系”二字就擅长处理关联。但实际上，这里的 relation 说的并不是关联（relationship），而是集合论里的概念。事实上，关系型数据库并不怎么擅长跨关系跳转。你必须设置外键，必须做 JOIN。一旦 JOIN 太多，场面就会彻底失控。

cues.en: If you've modeled a graph structure or a hierarchy, it's a special form of graph structure in a relational database, you'll have had this experience. It's not straightforward. Relational databases aren't good at this. So graph databases come in and say, yeah, we can handle jumping around relationships left, right, and center. We make it easy to do, and we optimize to make it fast to do that kind of thing. Furthermore, we can come up with an interesting
cues.zh: 如果你在关系型数据库中建模过图结构或层级结构（层级结构本质上是图结构的一种特例），你肯定深有体会。这并不简单，关系型数据库并不擅长这个。于是图数据库应运而生，它说：没事，我们可以轻松搞定错综复杂的关系跳转。我们让这种操作变得简单，并且专门优化保证速度。此外，我们还能设计出一种有趣的

cues.en: query language that is designed around allowing you to query graph structures. This kind of query here, this is Cypher from Neo4j, is all about saying, well, given a certain graph structure, let me use that graph structure to express a more complex query. And you can do some very interesting graph-oriented queries in graph databases, things that would be very, very difficult to write in terms of SQL.
cues.zh: 查询语言，专门用于查询图结构。就像这里的查询语句，这是 Neo4j 的 Cypher，其核心逻辑就是：给定某种图结构，利用该结构来表达更复杂的查询。你可以在图数据库中完成一些非常有趣的面向图的查询，而这些如果用 SQL 写起来会极其困难，

cues.en: as well as a pig in terms of performance. So, in many ways, you can kind of think of, we've gone in opposite directions. Aggregate-oriented databases take a lot of stuff that's scattered around and puts them into bigger lumps, while graph-oriented databases kind of break things apart into even smaller units and let you play with those smaller units more carefully. I mean, you can still model relationships in
cues.zh: 而且性能也会奇差无比。所以在许多方面你可以认为，这两者走向了截然相反的方向。面向聚合的数据库把分散的数据打包成更大的数据块，而面向图的数据库则把数据拆分成更小的单元，让你能更精细地操作它们。我是说，你依然可以在

cues.en: aggregate-oriented databases just as you can in relational databases. You basically refer to IDs in different documents, but it's a lot more messy. So part of your decision as to whether a NoSQL database is going to be interesting to you is how do you work with your data? Do you tend to work with the same aggregates all the time, which would lead you towards an aggregate-oriented approach?
cues.zh: 面向聚合的数据库中建模关联关系，就像在关系型数据库中一样。基本上就是引用不同文档中的 ID，但这要混乱得多。因此，决定 NoSQL 数据库是否适合你，部分取决于：你是如何使用数据的？你是否总是与固定的聚合数据打交道，从而引导你选择面向聚合的方案？

cues.en: Do you want to really break things up and jump across lots and lots of relationships in a complex structure that would lead you to a graph approach? Or is the tabular structure working well for you? In which case you want to stay with a relational approach. So NoSQL divides into those two categories. All of these are schema-less. So the graph databases as well allow you to add any bits of data to any node. You have all that flexibility, but with the same caution about implicit schemas as well.
cues.zh: 还是说你想彻底打散数据，并在复杂结构中跨越海量关联进行跳转，从而引导你选择图数据库？亦或是表格结构就已经很适合你？如果是这样，那你最好留在关系型方案上。所以 NoSQL 大致分为这两大类。它们全都是无 Schema 的。因此图数据库同样允许你给任何节点添加任意数据。你拥有完全的灵活性，但同样需要警惕隐式 Schema 的问题。

cues.en: So that is kind of half of the picture, the data model part. Now I'm going to move on to another issue, which is about consistency and effectively dealing with lots of people trying to modify the same data at the same time. You've probably heard something like this, that relational databases, they are ACID. They do the familiar ACID transactions that we all know and love. Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.
cues.zh: 这就是全貌的一半，即数据模型部分。现在我要讲另一个问题，那就是一致性，以及如何有效应对多人同时尝试修改同一数据的情况。你可能听过这种说法：关系型数据库是满足 ACID 的。它们支持大家都熟知且喜爱的 ACID 事务：原子性、一致性、隔离性、持久性。

cues.en: No sequel, they don't do any of that kind of thing. And of course, no sequel people will say, oh, we do base, which is an even more contrived and meaningless acronym than acid is. And I won't even attempt to tell you what it is because I can only remember what it is on Tuesdays. But basically what it boils down to is if you've got a single unit of information and you want to split it across several tables,
cues.zh: NoSQL 不做这类事情。当然，NoSQL 派会说：哦，我们支持 BASE，一个比 ACID 更牵强、更没意义的缩写。我甚至都不打算告诉你它是什么，因为我只有周二才记得住。但基本上，归根结底就是：如果你有一份信息，想把它拆到多张表里，

cues.en: What you don't want to be doing is caught in a position where you only get to write half the data and somebody else reads it. Or you get to write half the data and somebody takes the same order and writes a different half of the data and things get really messy. In that kind of situation, you need to have this mechanism to control, to effectively give you atomic updates. And that's really what transactions are all about. Atomic updates so that you either succeed or fail and nobody kind of comes in the middle and messes things up.
cues.zh: 你最不想遇到的情况就是：只写了一半数据，别人却读到了。或者你只写了一半数据，别人拿同一个订单写了另一半，事情变得一团糟。这种情况下，你需要一种控制机制，实际上就是给你原子更新。这正是事务的意义。原子更新，要么成功要么失败，没人中途插进来搞乱。

cues.en: Now, when it comes to our nicely organized set of NoSQL databases, the first thing to point out is graph databases do tend to follow ACID updates, which makes sense. They decompose the data even more than relational databases do, so they've got even more of a need to make sure they use transactions to wrap things together. So if anybody tells you, oh, NoSQL databases, they don't do ACID, you now know an immediate rejoinder.
cues.zh: 现在看我们整理好的 NoSQL 数据库分类，首先要指出，图数据库确实往往遵循 ACID 更新，这很合理。它们比关系型数据库更细地分解数据，所以更需要用事务把操作包在一起。所以如果有人告诉你，NoSQL 数据库不支持 ACID，你现在就知道怎么立刻反驳。

cues.en: Ah, but graph databases do. Now, aggregate-oriented databases, they actually don't need transactions as much because the aggregate is a kind of bigger, more richer structure. In fact, if you read the domain-driven design book, one of the things they point out is that the aggregates in domain-driven design are transaction boundaries. You shouldn't let transactions cross aggregate boundaries.
cues.zh: 啊，但图数据库就做。再看面向聚合的数据库，它们其实没那么需要事务，因为聚合是一种更大、更丰富的结构。事实上，如果你读过领域驱动设计那本书，其中一点就是：领域驱动设计中的聚合就是事务边界。你不应该让事务跨聚合边界。

cues.en: Because if you do, it'll just be complicated to manage the concurrence of your system. So the domain-driven design community, from the beginning, even before NoSQL said, keep your transactions within a single aggregate. And that's effectively what you do in the world of aggregate-oriented databases. Any aggregate's update is going to be atomic. It's going to be isolated. It's going to be consistent within itself.
cues.zh: 因为如果跨了，管理系统的并发就会变得很复杂。所以领域驱动设计社区从一开始，甚至在 NoSQL 出现之前就说：把事务保持在单个聚合内。面向聚合的数据库实际上就是这么做的。任何聚合的更新都是原子的，是隔离的，并在自身内部保持一致。

cues.en: It's only when you update multiple documents in a document or in database that you have to worry about the fact that you haven't got ACID transactions. But that problem occurs much more rarely than you'd think. So that's the first line about ACID-based think. Some databases are fully ACID anyway, and the aggregate-oriented databases that aren't, they are ACID within their aggregates, which is kind of what really matters.
cues.zh: 只有当你更新文档数据库中的多个文档时，才需要担心自己没有 ACID 事务。但这个问题出现得比你想象少得多。所以这是关于 ACID 思维的第一条。有些数据库本来就是完全 ACID 的；而那些不是的面向聚合数据库，在聚合内部是 ACID 的，而这才是真正重要的。

cues.en: But there's also a bit more to thinking about consistency even than that. Because even in a relational world, ACID transactions don't mean we get to be completely consistent and don't have to worry about update anomalies. And I will walk you through what hopefully is a very familiar scenario to point this out and also to illustrate how you deal with some of this. So imagine we have some typical multi-layered system. We've got a person talking to a browser, browser talks to a server, server talks to a single database.
cues.zh: 不过，关于一致性，还要想得比这更多一点。因为即便在关系型世界里，ACID 事务也不意味着我们就能做到完全一致、不用操心更新异常。我会带你看一个希望是非常熟悉的场景，来说明这一点，也说明你该如何处理其中一些问题。设想我们有一个典型的多层系统。一个人和浏览器交互，浏览器和服务器交互，服务器和单个数据库交互。

cues.en: And we're going to have two people talking to the same data in the same database at the same time, although through different browsers and servers. And here's the basic little scenario. We begin with both people, left and right, taking the same piece of data with a GET request, essentially. They bring it up onto the browser screen, and now the human being goes, I need to make some changes to this. And eventually, the guy on the
cues.zh: 我们会有两个人同时与同一个数据库中的同一份数据交互，不过是通过不同的浏览器和服务器。基本的小场景是这样的。开始时，左边和右边两个人都通过 GET 请求，本质上就是取同一份数据。他们把它加载到浏览器屏幕上，然后这个人说，我得改改这个。最终，那个……

cues.en: Left, I always get my left and right confused, says, OK, I've got my updated data, let's post some changes. And then shortly afterwards, the guy on the right says, hmm, I've uploaded my data now, let's post some changes. Now, of course, if we let that happen just like that, warning, conflict, this is a right-right conflict. Two people have updated the same piece of information. They weren't aware of each other's update, and they've got themselves in trouble. Acid to the rescue, right?
cues.zh: 左边的人——我总把左右搞混——说：“好，我的数据更新好了，发点改动上去吧。”然后没过多久，右边的人说：“嗯，我现在数据也上传好了，发点改动上去吧。”当然，如果我们就这么让它发生，警告，冲突，这是写-写冲突。两个人更新了同一条信息。他们不知道对方也更新了，结果把自己搞进麻烦里。ACID 来救场，对吧？

cues.en: What do we do? Well, what we have to do to prevent this conflict is we wrap the entire interaction from getting the data onto the screen and posting it back again in a transaction. That way, we make sure the database will ensure that we don't get a conflict. Effectively, one of them will be told, now you've got to do this again, retrieve your data again. We don't get conflicts. Problem solved. How many people do this on your production systems? Yeah. Occasionally, you can get away with this.
cues.zh: 那我们怎么办？要防止这种冲突，就得把整个交互——从取数据到屏幕上，再提交回去——包在一个事务里。这样，我们确保数据库会保证不出现冲突。实际上，其中一个人会被告知：现在你得重做一遍，重新取你的数据。这样就没有冲突。问题解决。你们生产系统上有多少人这么做？对。偶尔，你能侥幸这么干。

cues.en: Most of the time, you can't. Why? Because holding a transaction open for that length of time, while you've got a user looking and updating the data through the UI, that's going to really suck your performance out of your system. And I want to stress, you can do this in some circumstances. If your performance needs a really very minor, you've only got a handful of people looking at using the system at once,
cues.zh: 大多数时候，你做不到。为什么？因为把事务打开那么长时间，同时用户还在通过 UI 查看和更新数据，这会严重榨干你系统的性能。我想强调，有些情况下你可以这么做。如果你的性能需求真的很小，同时只有少数几个人在用这个系统，

cues.en: you might be able to get away with this approach. And it is advantageous to do so because a whole lot of problems go away if you do this. But for most systems, you can't afford to. You can't afford to hold transactions open that long. And in fact, most people who write about building systems like this will tell you never to do this. Don't hold transactions open for a user interaction. What they say instead is you just wrap the transaction around that update.
cues.zh: 你也许就能侥幸采用这种做法。而且这么做有好处，因为很多问题都会消失。但对大多数系统来说，你负担不起。你负担不起把事务打开那么久。事实上，大多数写这类系统构建文章的人都会告诉你永远别这么做。不要为了用户交互而让事务保持打开。他们说的是，你只需把事务包在那次更新上。

cues.en: that last bit of updating the database. And that's a good thing because that stops a collision where one half-done update mixes up with another half-done update and you get some tables updated over here and some different tables updated differently over there and the result is an inconsistent mess. But you still effectively get a conflict because the two people made updates of the same piece of information without knowing the other person did that.
cues.zh: 更新数据库的最后一步。这是件好事，因为它避免了冲突——即一个未完成的更新与另一个未完成的更新混在一起，导致这边的表更新了一部分，那边的表又按另一种方式更新，最终搞成一团不一致的乱麻。但实际上你依然会遇到冲突，因为两个人在彼此不知情的情况下修改了同一份数据。

cues.en: And this is what typically might happen, even in an aggregate-oriented database, if you have to modify more than one aggregate. Because you might find one person modifies the first one, and then they go over to the second one, the other person does it the other way around, and as a result you could lead into an inconsistent between aggregates. Now, if you've come across this, which you probably have, you probably also know how to solve this. And basically you use a technique which
cues.zh: 即使在面向聚合的数据库中，如果你需要修改多个聚合，这种情况也是经常发生的。因为可能一个人先改了第一个聚合，接着去改第二个；另一个人却按相反的顺序改，结果就会导致聚合之间的数据不一致。如果你遇到过这种情况（很可能遇到过），你也大概知道该怎么解决。基本上你会用到一种技术，

cues.en: In one of my previous books, I referred to as an offline lock. Basically, what that means, the usual way of implementing this, is that you give each data record, or each aggregate at least, a version stamp. And when you retrieve it, you retrieve the version stamp with the aggregate data. When you post, you provide the version stamp of where you read from. And then for the first guy, everything works at OK. The version stamp gets incremented.
cues.zh: 我在之前的一本书里称之为“离线锁”（offline lock）。它基本上意味着，或者说通常的实现方式是，给每条数据记录、或者至少每个聚合加一个版本戳。当你读取聚合数据时，顺便带出版本戳。当你提交更新时，带上你当初读取时的版本戳。对于先提交的那个人，一切顺利，版本戳递增。

cues.en: And then when the second person tries to post, they still got the old version stamp, and then you know something's up. And you can do whatever conflict resolution approach that you take. You use the same basic techniques, again, you're working with a NoSQL database. The nice thing is you don't have to worry about transactions about this problem so much, because the aggregate gives you that natural unit of update. It is your transaction boundary. But once you cross aggregates,
cues.zh: 接着当第二个人尝试提交时，他拿的还是旧版本戳，这时你就知道出问题了。然后你可以执行你所采用的任何冲突解决策略。在 NoSQL 数据库里，你同样会用到这些基础技术。好处是你不太需要为这个问题操心事务，因为聚合为你提供了天然的更新单元，它就是你的事务边界。但一旦跨越了聚合，

cues.en: then you've got to think about juggling version stamps and doing something of that kind. But it's not really very different to what you have to do with a relational database, because offline locks force you to do this juggling with version stamps anyway. So, yeah, you don't get these ACID transactions to the same degree that you do with a relational database, but the impact is not as great as some people think, because we actually have to deal with this stuff all the time anyway. Now, when we talk about consistency,
cues.zh: 你就得考虑怎么去协调版本戳以及类似的操作了。但这与你在关系型数据库里的做法并没有太大区别，因为离线锁本来就迫使你要去处理版本戳。所以，虽然你无法像在关系型数据库中那样获得同等程度的 ACID 事务，但影响并没有某些人想象的那么大，因为我们平时本来就一直在处理这类问题。现在，当我们谈到一致性时，

cues.en: I find it useful to think about actually two kinds of consistency. The consistency I've been talking about so far is what I call logical consistency. These consistency issues occur whether you're running on a cluster of machines or whether you're running on one single machine. You always have to worry about these kinds of consistency issues. Now, when you start spreading data across multiple machines, this can introduce more problems. When it comes to distributing data,
cues.zh: 我认为从两种一致性来思考会很有帮助。到目前为止我所说的一致性，我称之为“逻辑一致性”。无论你是在机器集群上运行，还是在单台机器上运行，这些一致性问题都会出现。你始终需要考虑这类一致性问题。而当你开始将数据分散到多台机器上时，就会引入更多的问题。说到分布式数据，

cues.en: Broadly, you can talk about it in two different ways. One is sharding data, taking one copy of the data and putting it on different machines, so that each piece of data lives in only one place, but you're using lots of machines. Sharding doesn't really change the picture very much. You still get the same logical consistency problems that you do with a single machine. They're exacerbated to some degree, but the basic problems are still the same. Another thing, however, that's common to do with clusters of machines is to replicate data.
cues.zh: 大致上可以分为两种方式。一种是数据分片（sharding），即把同一份数据拆开放到不同的机器上，每份具体数据只存在于一个地方，但你使用了许多机器。分片其实并没有太大改变大局。你依然会遇到与单机相同的逻辑一致性问题。在某种程度上它们被放大了，但基本问题仍然是一样的。然而，在机器集群中另一项常见的操作是数据复制。

cues.en: to put the same piece of data in lots of places. This can be advantageous in terms of performance, because now you've got more nodes handling the same set of requests. It can also be very valuable in terms of resilience. If one of your nodes goes down, the other replicas can still keep going. So hence, they'll talk a lot about availability and resilience with these cluster-oriented approaches. However, as soon as you replicate data, a new class of consistency problems starts coming in.
cues.zh: 把同一份数据存放在很多地方。从性能角度来看这很有优势，因为有更多的节点来处理同一批请求。从弹性角度来看也极具价值。如果其中一个节点宕机，其他副本依然能继续运行。因此，大家在讨论这些面向集群的方法时，经常会提到高可用性和弹性。然而，一旦复制了数据，一类全新的一致性问题就随之而来了。

cues.en: And again, illustrate with a simple example. So here we have two people, myself and my co-author Promote. And we both want to book a particular hotel room. And so we send in our booking request. And we happen to be on different continents. Promote's in India. I'm in the US. We send our requests to our local processing nodes. Now, the processing nodes at this point need to communicate.
cues.zh: 同样，我们用一个简单的例子来说明。这里有两个人，我和我的合著者 Promote。我们都想预订某一间特定的酒店房间。于是我们提交了预订请求。碰巧我们身处不同的大洲，Promote 在印度，我在美国。我们把请求发送到各自本地的处理节点。此时，这些处理节点之间就需要进行通信。

cues.en: We need to go, oh, hang on, what's going on here? And the system as a whole needs to come up with some kind of decision, essentially ensuring that one of us has to sleep on the streets. In this case, me. This is what happens 99.99 whatever percent of the time. However, let's take a kind of variation on this example. Again, we both want to book our hotel room, but now the communication line has gone down. The two nodes cannot communicate.
cues.zh: 它们得停下来搞清楚：“等等，这是怎么回事？”整个系统需要做出某种决断，基本上得确保我们俩当中有一个人去睡大街。在这个例子里，那个人是我。在 99.99% 或绝大多数情况下都是这样处理的。不过，我们来看这个例子的另一种变体。同样，我们都想预订这间房间，但现在通信链路断了，两个节点无法通信。

cues.en: We send in our requests. What happens? Well, actually, there's two broad alternatives. Alternative one is the system says, our communication line's gone down. Sorry, we can't take your hotel bookings at the moment. Please try again later. The alternative is the system says, yes, we'll accept your booking, thank you very much, because we're really reliable and up to date and all the rest of it. And they proceed to double book the hotel room. I'm not that friendly with Promote.
cues.zh: 我们发出了请求。接下来会发生什么？实际上大致有两种选择。方案一是系统说：“我们的通信线路断了。抱歉，目前无法处理您的酒店预订，请稍后再试。”另一种方案是系统说：“没问题，我们接受您的预订，非常感谢”，因为我们要保证高可靠、数据最新等等。接着他们就把这间房间重复预订了。我跟 Promote 可没熟到那个份上。

cues.en: We're good friends, but, you know, we're all in it. We may not want to share that hotel room. So, basically, what we're seeing is a choice. It's a choice between consistency, which means, you know, I'm not going to do anything if my communication line's down, and availability, which says, yes, I'm going to keep going, but at the risk of introducing an inconsistent behavior. There's a vital thing here to realize.
cues.zh: 我们是好朋友，但你懂的，我们可能并不想同住一间房间。所以基本上，我们面对的是一种抉择。这是在一致性（意味着如果通信中断，我就什么都不做）与可用性（意味着即便冒着出现不一致行为的风险，我也要继续提供服务）之间做选择。这里有一个必须认识到的关键点。

cues.en: is that this is a choice, and it's a choice that can only be made by knowing about the business rules, the domain rules that you're working with. I mean, it may sound really awful to say, oh, we're going to double book a hotel room, possibly with complete strangers. I mean, that would be bad. But actually, maybe the hotels have ways of dealing with this. Maybe they have a block of rooms that they always keep available till the last moment for emergencies. They can just use one of them.
cues.zh: 那就是：这是一种权衡，而且只能依据你所处理的业务规则和领域规则来做出抉择。听上去“把酒店房间重复预订，对方甚至可能是个完全陌生的人”确实很糟糕，那确实会很麻烦。但实际上，酒店或许有办法应对这种情况。也许他们始终保留着一批应急房间直到最后时刻，直接拿出一间来用就行了。

cues.en: Well, maybe they just send an apologetic groveling letter and some frequent sleeper points out to try and make me happy. There's various ways in business that people will deal with inconsistencies as they crop up. Now, I'm not saying you should always go for availability over consistency, but what is true is that it's always a domain choice. It is the business people who will have to decide. What's more important? The risk of double booking the last room in the hotel?
cues.zh: 嗯，也许他们只是寄来一封道歉信、低声下气地认错，再送点常旅客积分，想哄我开心。商业里，当不一致出现时，人们有各种处理方式。我不是说你应该总是选择可用性而不是一致性，但事实是，这始终是领域选择。得由业务人员来决定。哪个更重要？是酒店最后一间房被重复预订的风险？

cues.en: or the fact that we have to bring down the site and say, sorry, we can't accept any orders at the moment, which is kind of bad for business. This is one of the things that drove Dynamo. They wanted to make sure that the shopping cart was always available. You could always put things in the shopping cart. Why is this? Because it's America. What's the most important thing to do in America? Shopping. We must maintain our retail destiny. We must always be able to shop. And what happens?
cues.zh: 还是说，我们得把网站下线，说抱歉，目前不能接受订单——这对生意挺糟的。这正是推动 Dynamo 诞生的原因之一。他们想确保购物车始终可用。你总能往购物车里加东西。为什么？因为这是美国。在美国最重要的事是什么？购物。我们必须守住零售命运。我们必须永远能购物。然后会发生什么？

cues.en: You come to checkout and you go, why is this item in here twice? Or, I'm sure I put the so-and-so in here. Ah, computers, don't make mistakes, let me just fix it. When the worst is going to happen, you actually send out the order, you get duplicate stuff, you ring up Amazon. Sorry, sorry, sorry. And you get it all back. Much better than actually someone not being able to shop for a few seconds. So the point is, it's a business choice.
cues.zh: 你到结账时，会问：这东西怎么在这儿有两件？或者，我明明把某某放进去了。啊，计算机不会犯错，让我改一下。最糟的情况是，订单真发出去了，你收到重复的东西，打电话给 Amazon。对不起对不起对不起。然后全退回来。这比有人几秒钟不能购物要好得多。所以重点是，这是业务选择。

cues.en: So this then ties into something you'll hear endlessly about whenever someone talks about this stuff, which is the cap theorem. Everybody who's heard of the cap theorem? How many people understand the cap theorem? Some of you. It's actually pretty straightforward. It's described very badly though. Well, not very badly, but I don't think it's terribly useful. There's several of these three concepts up here and you get to pick any two. This is true, but I think it's easier to reformulate it.
cues.zh: 所以这就联系到你一谈这些就会没完没了听到的东西：CAP 定理。大家都听说过 CAP 定理吧？有多少人理解 CAP 定理？你们中有些人。其实它相当直接。只是描述得很糟。嗯，不是特别糟，但我觉得它没那么有用。这里有三个概念，你可以任选两个。这是对的，不过我觉得换种表述更容易。

cues.en: It's a bit clearer if you say, if you've got a system that can get a network partition, which basically means communication between different nodes in a cluster breaking down, and if you have a distributed system, by the way, you are going to get a network partitions. If you get a network partition, you have a choice. Do you want to be consistent or do you want to be available? And that's really what the CAP theorem boils down.
cues.zh: 如果你有一个可能发生网络分区的系统——基本上就是集群中不同节点之间的通信中断——而且，顺便说，只要你是分布式系统，就一定会遇到网络分区。一旦发生网络分区，你就得选择：要一致性，还是要可用性？CAP 定理归根结底就是这个。

cues.en: If you've got a single database running on a single server, it's not been a partition. You don't have to worry. You can be as available as that node is, and you're going to be consistent. You can maintain everything. But as soon as you have a distributed system, you have to make that choice. But that isn't a single binary choice right across your system. You actually have a spectrum. You can go for a certain amount. You can actually trade off levels of consistency and availability.
cues.zh: 如果只是一个跑在单台服务器上的单数据库，就不存在分区。你不用操心。这个节点有多可用，你就能有多可用，而且还能保持一致。你可以维持一切。但一旦有了分布式系统，你就必须做这个选择。不过这不是整个系统统一的一个二选一。实际上有一个连续谱。你可以选择某种程度，可以在一致性和可用性的水平之间做权衡。

cues.en: I'm not going to go into how, just me, you can. Furthermore, it can vary depending on a particular operation you want to do. Certain operations can be highly consistent, certain other operations can be highly available. Any of the databases that do this kind of stuff will give you all the knobs and tweaks to do this. And so you're going to learn out how to trade them across. And actually,
cues.zh: 我不会深入讲具体怎么做，我自己不展开，你们可以。而且，这取决于你要执行的具体操作。有些操作可以高度一致，另一些操作可以高度可用。任何做这类事情的数据库都会给你各种旋钮和调节项来实现。所以你要学会如何在它们之间做权衡。而实际上，

cues.en: Most of the time, you aren't trading off consistency versus availability. It's not availability that's the issue. And it's not even dealing with network partitions that's the issue. A lot of the time, what you're doing is you're trading off consistency versus response time. Because what's happening is the more you want to have consistency across a cluster of nodes, that means the more nodes have to get involved in the conversation. Again, think of that hotel case. The two had to communicate. That's going to slow down the response time.
cues.zh: 大多数时候，你并不是在一致性和可用性之间权衡。问题不在可用性。问题甚至也不在于处理网络分区。很多时候，你实际做的是在一致性和响应时间之间权衡。因为情况是，你越想在一个节点集群中实现一致性，就意味着越多节点必须参与通信。再想想那个酒店案例。这两方必须沟通。这就会拖慢响应时间。

cues.en: So you might say, even if the network is up, you know, I'm going to let each node book its own hotel stuff and sort it out later. Even with the network up, I'd still get you the faster response time rather than doing all the communication I need to get the consistency. And again, that's a business decision. Another thing that Amazon said was, we want to always get people shopping fast. Because what's the most important thing in America? Shopping.
cues.zh: 所以你可能会说，即使网络正常，我也要让每个节点自己订酒店，事后再处理。即使网络正常，我仍然能给你更快的响应时间，而不是做实现一致性所需的所有通信。再说一次，这是业务决策。Amazon还说的一件事是，我们要始终让人们快速购物。因为在美国最重要的事情是什么？购物。

cues.en: So therefore, we want really rapid times. And even if all the nodes are available and we could give you completely consistent solution, we want to be quick. And also, it helps that merging shopping carts, dealing with the inconsistency of shopping carts is relatively easy. Oh, they asked for this. Over here, they asked for that. Over there, well, clearly, they want both. Because this is America, everybody wants everything. Taking stuff out of shopping carts. Why would we want to encourage that?
cues.zh: 所以，我们想要非常快的速度。即使所有节点都可用，我们也能给你完全一致的方案，我们仍然要快。而且，合并购物车、处理购物车不一致相对容易，这也有帮助。哦，他们要求了这个。这边，他们要求了那个。那边，显然他们两者都想要。因为这是美国，每个人都想要一切。把东西从购物车里拿出来。我们为什么要鼓励那样？

cues.en: And in fact, this is a broader trade-off in terms of computing. This is really just another aspect of a general concurrency trade-off between safety and liveness. And if you've gone to concurrent classes and you've heard people talk about that, really this should actually seem fairly familiar in those kinds of terms. Now, what I really wanted to do with this little segment on consistency was focus on giving you a feel for how consistency is different in the
cues.zh: 而事实上，这是计算领域更广泛的权衡。这其实只是安全性与活性之间一般并发权衡的另一个方面。如果你上过并发课程，听过人们讨论这个，那么用这些术语来说，这应该显得相当熟悉。现在，我在这段关于一致性的小章节里真正想做的，是让你感受一致性在

cues.en: particularly the aggregate-oriented NoSQL world, as opposed to how you may have thought about consistency so far. There's a lot of topics I could have talked about here that I just haven't got time to talk about. The important thing to go away with is realizing that you have to think about consistency issues differently, essentially because you've got this different data model and the possibility of replicated data. And in particular, you have to think about
cues.zh: 尤其是面向聚合的NoSQL世界中，与你到目前为止可能对一致性的理解相比，有何不同。这里有很多主题我本可以讲，但就是没时间讲。你带走的重要一点是，要意识到你必须以不同方式思考一致性问题，本质上是因为你有不同的数据模型以及数据复制的可能性。尤其重要的是，你必须考虑

cues.en: this terms of this consistency availability trade-off. And that it's not up to just us as techies to make that decision. It is actually up to the way the business wanna works as to where we make these trade-offs. And if you want more, well, I'm gonna tell you to buy my book anyway, so you know what to do. Okay, so the last little segment, I'm gonna talk a bit about when and why you might want to use a NoSQL database.
cues.zh: 这种一致性与可用性之间的权衡。而且，做这个决定并不只是我们技术人员的事。实际上，我们到底在哪里做这些权衡，取决于业务希望如何运作。如果你想要更多内容，反正我会让你买我的书，所以你知道该怎么做。好，那么在最后一个小节，我会稍微讲讲什么时候以及为什么你可能想使用NoSQL数据库。

cues.en: And the way I think of it is there are two drivers that push us towards a NoSQL database. The first one is the one that I've already talked about as the real driver for the whole NoSQL movement itself. And that is you've got to deal with large amounts of data. If you've got more data than you can comfortably or economically fit onto a single database server, you're going to have to deal with some pain. You can either take the pain of trying to run a relational database across a cluster,
cues.zh: 我理解是，有两个因素推动我们采用 NoSQL 数据库。第一个我已经讲过，它也是整个 NoSQL 运动真正的推动力。那就是你必须处理海量数据。如果你的数据量超过单台数据库服务器能轻松或经济地承载的范围，你就得承受一些痛苦。你可以选择承受在集群上运行关系型数据库的痛苦，

cues.en: or you can go into this new NoSQL stuff. And most of the time, I think I'd go for the NoSQL stuff. Because running relational databases across clusters is still somewhat of a black art. So big amounts of data is a big issue. Now, some people have said, and one of the reviewers' comments on my book was, yeah, but only very few organizations have to worry about this stuff. If you Google and Amazon, yes. Pretty much everybody else, no. As I read that, what I heard in my head was,
cues.zh: 或者你可以去搞这些新的 NoSQL 东西。大多数时候，我觉得我会选 NoSQL。因为跨集群运行关系型数据库仍然有点像黑魔法。所以海量数据是个大问题。有人说过，而且我书的一位审稿人评论说：是啊，但只有极少数组织需要操心这些。如果你是 Google 和 Amazon，那确实。其他几乎所有人，不用。我读到这句话时，脑子里听到的是：

cues.en: 640K is enough for almost everybody. The reality is there is tons of data coming at us. And every organization is going to be capturing and processing more and more data. So this large-scale data problem, it's only going to grow. And that is a factor. But actually, this is not the main reason, I think, why most people go into NoSQL. There was a survey I saw in the track on Monday that pointed out that most people actually aren't interested in
cues.zh: 640K 对几乎所有人都够用了。现实是，海量数据正朝我们涌来。每个组织都会采集和处理越来越多的数据。所以这个大规模数据问题只会越来越大。这确实是一个因素。但实际上，我认为这并不是大多数人转向 NoSQL 的主要原因。周一我在分会场看到一项调查，它指出大多数人其实并不关心

cues.en: Big amounts of data from our SQL databases. What they want to do is they want to be able to develop more easily. So a good example of this is I have some friends who work on the Guardian newspaper and website. How many people have heard of the Guardian? Good English language newspaper. Many of you, good. And they're dealing with articles. They're saving articles, updating articles, pushing articles back and forth. The article for them is a natural aggregate.
cues.zh: 来自我们 SQL 数据库的海量数据。他们真正想要的是能够更轻松地进行开发。举个很好的例子，我有几个朋友在 Guardian 的报纸和网站工作。有多少人听说过 Guardian？一份很棒的英文报纸。很多人听过，很好。他们日常处理的就是文章。他们保存文章、更新文章、来回传递文章。对他们来说，文章就是一个天然的聚合。

cues.en: articles, data, and metadata across relational databases, it's a pain in the neck. It's awkward. But taking it as a single thing, a single article, and pushing it into the database, that's much more straightforward. The impedance mismatch problem is drastically reduced if you've got a natural aggregate. And many of the projects that I've talked to in ThoughtWorks that have used a NoSQL database have gone that route.
cues.zh: 跨关系型数据库去处理文章、数据和元数据，真是让人头疼，特别别扭。但如果把它当作一个整体，一篇单独的文章直接存进数据库，那就直接多了。只要有天然的聚合，阻抗失配问题就会大幅减轻。我在 ThoughtWorks 了解过的许多使用 NoSQL 数据库的项目，走的都是这条路。

cues.en: They've said, our data model doesn't really fit very well with relational. One of these NoSQL options is better. It might be a natural aggregate, in which case they've gone the aggregate-oriented route. Or it might be, we've got something that feels much like a graph structure, so we go the graph database route. And that, I think, is the most common reason at the moment why people are using NoSQL databases, because you're effectively getting rid of that impedance mismatch problem. Now, of course, that raises a question.
cues.zh: 他们说，我们的数据模型和关系型数据库不太契合，某个 NoSQL 方案会更好。它可能是一个自然的聚合，这种情况下他们就走面向聚合的路线。或者，我们手上的东西感觉很像图结构，于是就走图数据库路线。我认为，这是目前人们使用 NoSQL 数据库最常见的原因，因为你实际上消除了阻抗失配问题。当然，这就引出了一个问题。

cues.en: That was, of course, the promise of object databases. They were going to get rid of the impedance mismatch problem, but they got clobbered because databases are being used for integration. Why is that same problem not hitting us now? Well, it is hitting us, but it's greatly reduced because now more and more people are saying we don't want to integrate that way. We want to hide our databases inside a broader application or service, and then we want to use some kind of service-oriented interaction between the two.
cues.zh: 那当然是对象数据库的承诺。它们本要消除阻抗失配问题，但最终败下阵来，因为数据库正被用于集成。为什么同样的问题现在没有击中我们？嗯，它确实在击中我们，但已大大减轻，因为现在越来越多人说，我们不想再那样集成了。我们想把数据库藏在一个更广泛的应用或服务内部，然后在两者之间采用某种面向服务的交互。

cues.en: which may be web services, it can be something as really disgusting as soap on ESBs with God knows what thrown in. But the point is applications are now controlling access to data. And if you're in a scenario where you can do that, where you can effectively encapsulate your database, then the integration issue becomes a lot less serious. And that, I think, is a very important enabler to make it possible for NoSQL databases to thrive.
cues.zh: 这种交互可以是 Web 服务，也可以是极其恶心的东西，比如在 ESB 上跑 SOAP，还掺进天知道什么。但关键是，现在应用在控制对数据的访问。如果你处在能做到这一点的场景，能有效封装数据库，那么集成问题就变得没那么严重。我认为这是一个非常重要的推动因素，让 NoSQL 数据库得以繁荣。

cues.en: that this is a good practice anyway. Even if you've got relational databases, you do not wanna be integrating through integration databases. That cause no end of trouble, believe me, if you haven't experienced it yourself. So much better to try and encapsulate something like that. And if you're gonna do that, then you've got much more freedom for what database to use. And I think that's gonna be a very driving structure towards this. Another thing that's encouraging people to use,
cues.zh: 而且无论如何，这都是个好做法。即使你用的是关系数据库，也不该通过集成数据库来做集成。相信我，那会带来无穷无尽的麻烦——如果你自己没经历过的话。更好的做法是试着把这类东西封装起来。如果你这么做，那么选用什么数据库就有大得多的自由。我认为这会成为推动这件事的非常有力的因素。另一个促使人们使用

cues.en: These databases is to deal with analytics. We all know about data warehousing. The usual data warehousing project, as far as I can tell, is that Salesman turns up from one of the big companies and says, oh, you want to do data warehousing. Well, here's this project plan by which every piece of data you could possibly have in your organization is all put into one place so that everybody can get at it easily. And it's a multi-year project with lots and lots of very diverse stakeholders. We know that story.
cues.zh: 这些数据库的因素，是为了处理分析。我们都了解数据仓库。就我所见，通常的数据仓库项目是这样的：某家大公司的销售员跑来说，哦，你想做数据仓库。那好，这是一份项目计划，按照它，你组织里可能拥有的每一条数据都被放进同一个地方，好让所有人都能轻松拿到。而且这是个多年项目，牵扯大量形形色色的利益相关者。这套故事我们都懂。

cues.en: And people come across these big data warehousing projects that they felt have succeeded. There's usually one or two. No one's prepared to admit it. Oh, you're prepared to admit it. But most of them go badly. What we look for instead is a different approach that says, let's particularly focus on one particular problem.
cues.zh: 人们会遇到一些他们觉得成功的大型数据仓库项目。通常也就一两个。没人愿意承认。哦，你倒是愿意承认。但大多数项目都搞得很糟。我们转而寻找的是一种不同的做法：让我们特别聚焦于某个特定问题。

cues.en: and see how do we grab the data from that. And the data, by the way, might not be in well-known relational or even NoSQL stores. It might be scattered around in log files or what truly runs most enterprises, which is Excel spreadsheets. Well, let's get at that data and let's poke it and pull it together. And NoSQL databases play an important role in this. The graph databases allow you to easily do graph-like analytics on the database, which is really quite nice.
cues.zh: 然后看看我们怎么从那里抓取数据。顺便说，数据未必在知名的关系型甚至 NoSQL 存储里。它可能散落在日志文件里，或者散落在真正支撑大多数企业运转的东西里——Excel 电子表格。那好，让我们拿到这些数据，戳一戳，再把它拼起来。NoSQL 数据库在这方面扮演重要角色。图数据库让你能轻松在数据库上做类似图的分析，这确实相当不错。

cues.en: The aggregate-oriented databases are generally less good at this because they can't slice and dice so well, but what they can do is store large quantities of data. So if you are pulling stuff off devices or log files or the like, then they become very attractive. And of course, that's what's given a big advantage to Amazon because they're able to mine all this information. So with all of this, does this mean that NoSQL is the future of databases? That relational databases are going to disappear and we're all going to be doing
cues.zh: 面向聚合的数据库在这方面通常稍逊一筹，因为它们做多维切片分析没那么灵活，但它们的强项是存储海量数据。所以，如果你要从设备或日志文件之类的地方拉取数据，它们就非常有吸引力了。当然，这也给 Amazon 带来了巨大的优势，因为他们能够挖掘所有这些信息。那么说了这么多，这是否意味着 NoSQL 就是数据库的未来？关系型数据库将彻底消失，我们以后都要用

cues.en: No SQL stuff? I don't think so. I think really the future is something that I refer to as polyglot persistence. And what this means is we think that there's going to be room for lots and lots of different kinds of databases with relational databases still playing a big role. And if you're building an application, maybe you'll use lots of different databases as part of your application.
cues.zh: NoSQL 相关的技术了吗？我认为不会。我认为真正的未来是我所谓的“多语言持久化”（polyglot persistence）。这意味着我们认为会有很多很多不同类型的数据库共存，而关系型数据库依然会扮演重要角色。如果你在构建一个应用，你可能会在同一个应用中混合使用多种不同的数据库。

cues.en: Certainly, across an organization, you'll use lots of databases. And what you're doing is you're choosing the appropriate database for the nature of the problem that you're working with. And because there are different natures of problems, there are different data stores. But the idea of whatever your problem is, the answer is a relational database, will go away. Now, this is great. It gives us lots of opportunities for the future. But as every cynic knows, every opportunity is really a problem.
cues.zh: 当然，在整个组织架构层面，你会用到非常多的数据库。你要做的是根据所处理问题的本质，选择最合适的数据库。正因为问题类型千差万别，才会有各种不同的数据存储方案。但是，“不管遇到什么问题，答案一律是关系型数据库”的时代要结束了。这很棒，它为未来带来了大量机遇。但正如每个悲观主义者所知，每个机遇背后其实都是一个挑战。

cues.en: And there are plenty of them. You've now got to think about this kind of stuff. You've got to decide what is the appropriate NoSQL database for a problem. You've got to deal with organizational issues. Relational DBAs are not going to like this. In fact, for some people, that's a big advantage, but let's not go there. NoSQL databases are immature. They don't have the tools and the experience and the knowledge of how to work with them well that we've had from 20 years of relational databases.
cues.zh: 而且挑战还真不少。你现在必须开始操心这类事了：你得判断针对具体问题哪款 NoSQL 数据库才是最合适的；你还得应对组织架构上的阻力，关系型 DBA 们肯定不会喜欢它。事实上对某些人来说这反而是个大优势，但我们先不扯远了。NoSQL 数据库还不够成熟，我们在关系型数据库上积累了 20 年的配套工具、实践经验和专业认知，而 NoSQL 目前还很欠缺。

cues.en: And all of these consistency issues can still end up biting you. So when it comes to what kind of project, I start with the drivers. If you want rapid time to market, fast cycle time, you need to be quick, easier development is really important. Therefore, if you can do that with NoSQL databases, that's the reason to go with them. Similarly, if you've got a very data intensive project, then obviously NoSQL's ability to deal with large amounts of data is very important.
cues.zh: 而且所有这些一致性问题最后都可能让你栽跟头。所以说到适用于什么样的项目，我会先看驱动因素。如果你想要产品迅速上市、快速迭代、必须争分夺秒，那么更轻松的开发体验就至关重要。因此，如果 NoSQL 数据库能帮你做到这一点，那就是选用它们的理由。同样，如果你面对的是一个数据密集型项目，那么 NoSQL 处理海量数据的能力显然就非常关键。

cues.en: But I think there's another overriding goal as well, which is, is your project really important to the competitive advantage of your business? What I refer to as a strategic project. Because if it's a strategic project, then it's worth taking on the extra risk, the unknowns of dealing with an immature and not so well-known technology, which is what no sequels are.
cues.zh: 但我认为还有一个更核心的目标，那就是：你的项目对企业的核心竞争优势是否真的至关重要？也就是我所谓的“战略级项目”。因为如果是战略级项目，那就值得去承担额外的风险，去直面一项不够成熟、认知度还不高的新技术带来的未知数——而这恰恰就是 NoSQL 目前的现状。

cues.en: If, on the other hand, you've got a project that's what I call a utility project, it's kind of a straightforward, it's not really vital to the business's operation, then that may be not the best place to bring in an unknown like this. In that kind of situation, you're probably better off with a familiar, at least for a few years. But there's lots of strategic projects out there, and certainly our experience over the last two or three years at ThoughtWorks has been very positive.
cues.zh: 另一方面，如果你的项目属于我所说的“工具型项目”，逻辑比较简单直接，对核心业务运营也不是特别关键，那可能就不是引入这种未知技术的最佳场景。在这种情况下，至少在未来几年内，坚持用熟悉的技术可能会更稳妥。但市面上还有很多战略级项目，而且从我们过去两三年在 ThoughtWorks 的实践来看，效果非常积极。

cues.en: with NoSQL databases. I've heard remarkably few complaints. And thought workers always complain about what they're working with. So I certainly am very much convinced that NoSQL databases have an important part to play in the spectrum of future developments. And the rest of the talks in this track will explore different ways in which they've been used. So I hope you found that helpful. If you want more depth, the book is very thin.
cues.zh: ——尤其是在使用 NoSQL 数据库方面。我很少听到抱怨，要知道 ThoughtWorks 的员工向来很喜欢吐槽手头用的工具。所以我非常确信，NoSQL 数据库在未来的技术版图中必定会扮演重要角色。本专题接下来的演讲也会探讨它们的各种实际应用方式。希望这些内容对大家有所帮助。如果你想了解更深入的内容，那本书其实很薄。

cues.en: My target was 150 pages, and I only missed it by two, so it's 152 pages. Quick overview, a bit more than what I just gave you, and I hope that will be handy. If you've got that page on my website, I collect together various other things that I've done or talked about in terms of NoSQL. And thank you for listening to me.
cues.zh: 我最初的目标是 150 页，最后只差了两页，全书只有 152 页。它是一个快速概览，比我刚才讲的内容更丰富一些，希望能对大家派上用场。如果你们访问我网站上的那个页面，那里汇总了我关于 NoSQL 做过的其他内容和演讲。感谢大家的聆听！
